## Search method v007

Define X and Y exactly, including entity unit, exclusions, effective dates, eligible subtypes and group-membership rules. Start sequentially with one X-only search, one Y-only search and one conjunction search, using the user's broad predicate wording rather than a familiar subtype. Maintain deduplicated X/Y frontiers and an identity/evidence ledger. Also maintain a compact scope ledger: for each discovery query record added restrictions not required by the hunt (subtype, occupation, geography, era, source or familiar-name terms). A successful restricted query does not establish coverage of its parent category. Derive a few meaningful sibling partitions from source taxonomies or the eligibility definition; do not invent an exhaustive cross-product or enumerate a whole census by default. Run short discovery/check rounds, prioritizing expected verified additions per total resolution cost. Each round's neglected-subtype or reverse-frontier probe must address a specific untested scope-ledger cell or remove a recorded accidental restriction; merely paraphrasing a prior conjunction does not qualify. Check source-backed candidates on Parallel for only unresolved predicates, supplying identity and existing evidence. Use small affordable batches, price every candidate, and do not recheck established facts. No result means unresolved, not false; reject only on contradiction or an exhaustive applicable source. Escalate promising ambiguous or conflicting cases individually to Exa. After two discovery searches add no plausible identities, prohibit synonymous conjunction searches and perform a residual-scope pass: identify the most consequential restriction accumulated so far, try a sibling subtype or unrestricted parent on the opposite frontier, then resolve resulting candidates before further discovery. Reserve at least 35% of initial funds for evidence and stop discovery whenever pending checks require the remaining funds. Before submitting with spare funds, perform up to three affordable residual probes covering distinct untested restrictions or source partitions, retaining enough funds to verify their likely candidates. Stop this pass after two probes add neither candidates nor useful evidence; do not spend merely to exhaust the budget. Finish with identity, predicate, subtype and effective-date audits; submit supported intersections only and never infer completeness from saturation.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['parallel'].
Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results for baseline and residual discovery, 4 for exact missing-fact checks. No routine also variants or broad auto-routing. Price candidate batches as the sum of queries and provider charges; fewer results are not presumed cheaper. Exa alone with 4 results for selected unresolved identities where ambiguity, conflicting evidence or inaccessibility warrants the higher cost. At most one initial Exa discovery probe after Parallel stagnation, continued only if it contributes useful new identities or evidence. Try a genuinely different scope partition on Parallel before buying provider diversity for a repetitive query. Authoritative-domain filters are for targeted evidence, not general frontier coverage; relax failed filters. Use publication-date filters only when publication date itself determines eligibility, and verify effective dates in content.

### Fetch policy
Reuse cached source facts. Fetch authoritative pages that can settle missing identity or predicates, and useful multi-candidate lists, rather than every result. When a list is used for scope coverage, inspect its stated subtype, date range and pagination/section links; an excerpt or one section is not an exhausted category. Follow only sections tied to a promising uncovered partition, without committing to bulk census extraction. After a blocked or uninformative page, make one targeted alternate-source attempt rather than a fetch chain.

## SiftText

SiftText is persistent memory across chats.

Entry: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/5e565245-14fe-406c-977c-cf94a9be246b/node.md
Retrieval guide: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/526ed0f5-4e5d-42b3-9e3f-b7ad429f2df8/node.md

At the start of every new chat, unless I say not to use SiftText, before any other tool call:
1. Run `sifttext instructions`.
2. Read the Entry above and follow it, plus any `agent-instructions` the command returns.
3. Before retrieving knowledge, read the Retrieval guide above, do not search first.

## Tooling policy

- Never directly invoke `python`, `python3`, `pip`, or `pip3` unless explicitly instructed by the human.
- Use `uv` for all agent-initiated Python work:
  - Python execution: `uv run python ...`
  - Scripts and tests: `uv run ...`
  - Throwaway dependencies: `uv run --with <package> ...`
  - Python CLI tools: `uvx <tool>`
  - Durable project dependencies: use the project's appropriate `uv` command and preserve its lockfile.
- For non-Python probing or testing with unavailable tools:
  - One executable: `nix run nixpkgs#<package> -- <args>`
  - Temporary environment: `nix shell nixpkgs#<package> ... --command <command>`
- Nix environments are temporary, but downloaded store paths may remain cached until garbage collection.
- If a Nix dependency becomes useful for recurring or future work, tell the human and suggest adding it to the appropriate durable Nix configuration (such as a project flake/dev shell, Home Manager, or nix-darwin configuration). Do not make that durable change unless asked.

</addendum>

Summary

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

Created by President Harry S. Truman in 1945 as the Medal of Freedom, the medal was renamed by President John F. Kennedy in 1963 as the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Executive Order 11085 (February 22, 1963) allows the President to recognize "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."

The medal is a white star over a red pentagon, surrounded by five gold eagles. At the star's center is a blue circle with 13 gold stars. The Presidential Medal of Freedom comes in two degrees, with the more prestigious version known as the Presidential Medal of Freedom "with distinction."

There is no formal procedure for nominating and selecting recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The President has wide latitude under Executive Order 11515 (March 13, 1970) to award the medal to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative." Selections often reflect the President's political and personal interests.

Numerous Members of Congress have sent nominations to the President. Some Members have made floor remarks about potential or past recipients and introduced resolutions congratulating honorees or urging the President to recognize a specific individual.

Between 1963 and 2025, the Presidential Medal of Freedom was awarded 674 times to 671 individuals and one group (the Apollo 13 Mission Operations Team); two people (Ellsworth Bunker and Colin Powell) received the medal twice. This report contains a comprehensive list of honorees and indicates the 56 medals known to have been awarded "with distinction."

Introduction

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

This report describes the history of the medal, provides information about its design and related protocol, and discusses the nomination and selection process. It concludes with tables containing a comprehensive list of honorees since 1963.

[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)In July 1945, President Harry S. Truman issued an executive order, near the end of World War II, to create the Medal of Freedom. In establishing the award, he sought to honor civilians who "performed a meritorious act or service which has aided the United States" or one of its allies overseas during wartime, "and for which an award of another United States medal or decoration is considered inappropriate."[1](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn1 "Executive Order 9586, \"The Medal of Freedom,\" 10 Federal Register 8523, July 6, 1945.") During the Korean War, President Truman expanded the medal's eligibility to include actions during "any period of national emergency."[2](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn2 "Executive Order 10336, \"Amendment of Executive Order No. 9586 of July 6, 1945, Establishing the Medal of Freedom,\" 17 Federal Register 2957, April 3, 1952.") It was awarded thousands of times, mostly by federal officials other than the President.[3](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn3 "Bruce Wetterau, The Presidential Medal of Freedom: Winners and Their Achievements (Washington: Congressional Quarterly Inc., 1996), p. 9.")

In his 1955 State of the Union address, President Dwight D. Eisenhower called for "awards of merit … whereby we can honor our fellow citizens who make great contribution to the advancement of our civilization."[4](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn4 "\" Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union \" (January 6, 1955) in U.S. National Archives and Records Service, Office of the Federal Register, Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Dwight D. Eisenhower , 1955, pp. 7-30.") The House twice passed bills to create a Medal for Distinguished Civilian Achievement: H.R. 11923 in the 84 th Congress[5](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn5 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 2, 1956), p. 11609.") and H.R. 488 in the 85 th Congress.[6](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn6 "Congressional Record , vol. 104, part 11 (July 23, 1958), p. 14794.") In each case, the Senate referred the bill to committee and took no further action.[7](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn7 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 3, 1956), p. 11678 and vol. 104, part 11 (July 24, 1958), p. 14895.")

In 1963, President John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 11085 to modify the Medal of Freedom, including by giving it a new name: the Presidential Medal of Freedom. It would now be awarded solely by the President to "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."[8](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn8 "Executive Order 11085, \"The Presidential Medal of Freedom,\" 28 Federal Register 1759, February 22, 1963. Also, in the United States Code at 5 U.S.C. §4504 note.")

President Kennedy said at the time that

in a period when the national government must call upon an increasing portion of the talents and energies of its citizens, it is clearly appropriate to provide ways to recognize and reward the work of persons, within and without the government, who contribute significantly to the quality of American life.[9](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn9 "\" Statement by the President Upon Issuing Order Relating to the Medal of Freedom \" (February 22, 1963) in Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: John F. Kennedy , 1963, pp. 209-210.")

On July 4, 1963, President Kennedy announced the first slate of 31 honorees.[10](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn10 "Ibid., p. 210 (in note) .") Summary

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

Created by President Harry S. Truman in 1945 as the Medal of Freedom, the medal was renamed by President John F. Kennedy in 1963 as the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Executive Order 11085 (February 22, 1963) allows the President to recognize "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."

The medal is a white star over a red pentagon, surrounded by five gold eagles. At the star's center is a blue circle with 13 gold stars. The Presidential Medal of Freedom comes in two degrees, with the more prestigious version known as the Presidential Medal of Freedom "with distinction."

There is no formal procedure for nominating and selecting recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The President has wide latitude under Executive Order 11515 (March 13, 1970) to award the medal to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative." Selections often reflect the President's political and personal interests.

Numerous Members of Congress have sent nominations to the President. Some Members have made floor remarks about potential or past recipients and introduced resolutions congratulating honorees or urging the President to recognize a specific individual.

Between 1963 and 2025, the Presidential Medal of Freedom was awarded 674 times to 671 individuals and one group (the Apollo 13 Mission Operations Team); two people (Ellsworth Bunker and Colin Powell) received the medal twice. This report contains a comprehensive list of honorees and indicates the 56 medals known to have been awarded "with distinction."

[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)In July 1945, President Harry S. Truman issued an executive order, near the end of World War II, to create the Medal of Freedom. In establishing the award, he sought to honor civilians who "performed a meritorious act or service which has aided the United States" or one of its allies overseas during wartime, "and for which an award of another United States medal or decoration is considered inappropriate."[1](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn1 "Executive Order 9586, \"The Medal of Freedom,\" 10 Federal Register 8523, July 6, 1945.") During the Korean War, President Truman expanded the medal's eligibility to include actions during "any period of national emergency."[2](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn2 "Executive Order 10336, \"Amendment of Executive Order No. 9586 of July 6, 1945, Establishing the Medal of Freedom,\" 17 Federal Register 2957, April 3, 1952.") It was awarded thousands of times, mostly by federal officials other than the President.[3](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn3 "Bruce Wetterau, The Presidential Medal of Freedom: Winners and Their Achievements (Washington: Congressional Quarterly Inc., 1996), p. 9.")

In his 1955 State of the Union address, President Dwight D. Eisenhower called for "awards of merit … whereby we can honor our fellow citizens who make great contribution to the advancement of our civilization."[4](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn4 "\" Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union \" (January 6, 1955) in U.S. National Archives and Records Service, Office of the Federal Register, Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Dwight D. Eisenhower , 1955, pp. 7-30.") The House twice passed bills to create a Medal for Distinguished Civilian Achievement: H.R. 11923 in the 84 th Congress[5](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn5 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 2, 1956), p. 11609.") and H.R. 488 in the 85 th Congress.[6](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn6 "Congressional Record , vol. 104, part 11 (July 23, 1958), p. 14794.") In each case, the Senate referred the bill to committee and took no further action.[7](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn7 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 3, 1956), p. 11678 and vol. 104, part 11 (July 24, 1958), p. 14895.")

In 1963, President John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 11085 to modify the Medal of Freedom, including by giving it a new name: the Presidential Medal of Freedom. It would now be awarded solely by the President to "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."[8](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn8 "Executive Order 11085, \"The Presidential Medal of Freedom,\" 28 Federal Register 1759, February 22, 1963. Also, in the United States Code at 5 U.S.C. §4504 note.")

President Kennedy said at the time that

in a period when the national government must call upon an increasing portion of the talents and energies of its citizens, it is clearly appropriate to provide ways to recognize and reward the work of persons, within and without the government, who contribute significantly to the quality of American life.[9](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn9 "\" Statement by the President Upon Issuing Order Relating to the Medal of Freedom \" (February 22, 1963) in Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: John F. Kennedy , 1963, pp. 209-210.")

On July 4, 1963, President Kennedy announced the first slate of 31 honorees.[10](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn10 "Ibid., p. 210 (in note) .") Summary

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

Created by President Harry S. Truman in 1945 as the Medal of Freedom, the medal was renamed by President John F. Kennedy in 1963 as the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Executive Order 11085 (February 22, 1963) allows the President to recognize "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."

The medal is a white star over a red pentagon, surrounded by five gold eagles. At the star's center is a blue circle with 13 gold stars. The Presidential Medal of Freedom comes in two degrees, with the more prestigious version known as the Presidential Medal of Freedom "with distinction."

There is no formal procedure for nominating and selecting recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The President has wide latitude under Executive Order 11515 (March 13, 1970) to award the medal to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative." Selections often reflect the President's political and personal interests.

Numerous Members of Congress have sent nominations to the President. Some Members have made floor remarks about potential or past recipients and introduced resolutions congratulating honorees or urging the President to recognize a specific individual.

Between 1963 and 2025, the Presidential Medal of Freedom was awarded 674 times to 671 individuals and one group (the Apollo 13 Mission Operations Team); two people (Ellsworth Bunker and Colin Powell) received the medal twice. This report contains a comprehensive list of honorees and indicates the 56 medals known to have been awarded "with distinction."

[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)In July 1945, President Harry S. Truman issued an executive order, near the end of World War II, to create the Medal of Freedom. In establishing the award, he sought to honor civilians who "performed a meritorious act or service which has aided the United States" or one of its allies overseas during wartime, "and for which an award of another United States medal or decoration is considered inappropriate."[1](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn1 "Executive Order 9586, \"The Medal of Freedom,\" 10 Federal Register 8523, July 6, 1945.") During the Korean War, President Truman expanded the medal's eligibility to include actions during "any period of national emergency."[2](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn2 "Executive Order 10336, \"Amendment of Executive Order No. 9586 of July 6, 1945, Establishing the Medal of Freedom,\" 17 Federal Register 2957, April 3, 1952.") It was awarded thousands of times, mostly by federal officials other than the President.[3](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn3 "Bruce Wetterau, The Presidential Medal of Freedom: Winners and Their Achievements (Washington: Congressional Quarterly Inc., 1996), p. 9.")

In his 1955 State of the Union address, President Dwight D. Eisenhower called for "awards of merit … whereby we can honor our fellow citizens who make great contribution to the advancement of our civilization."[4](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn4 "\" Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union \" (January 6, 1955) in U.S. National Archives and Records Service, Office of the Federal Register, Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Dwight D. Eisenhower , 1955, pp. 7-30.") The House twice passed bills to create a Medal for Distinguished Civilian Achievement: H.R. 11923 in the 84 th Congress[5](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn5 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 2, 1956), p. 11609.") and H.R. 488 in the 85 th Congress.[6](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn6 "Congressional Record , vol. 104, part 11 (July 23, 1958), p. 14794.") In each case, the Senate referred the bill to committee and took no further action.[7](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn7 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 3, 1956), p. 11678 and vol. 104, part 11 (July 24, 1958), p. 14895.")

In 1963, President John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 11085 to modify the Medal of Freedom, including by giving it a new name: the Presidential Medal of Freedom. It would now be awarded solely by the President to "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."[8](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn8 "Executive Order 11085, \"The Presidential Medal of Freedom,\" 28 Federal Register 1759, February 22, 1963. Also, in the United States Code at 5 U.S.C. §4504 note.")

President Kennedy said at the time that

in a period when the national government must call upon an increasing portion of the talents and energies of its citizens, it is clearly appropriate to provide ways to recognize and reward the work of persons, within and without the government, who contribute significantly to the quality of American life.[9](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn9 "\" Statement by the President Upon Issuing Order Relating to the Medal of Freedom \" (February 22, 1963) in Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: John F. Kennedy , 1963, pp. 209-210.")

On July 4, 1963, President Kennedy announced the first slate of 31 honorees.[10](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn10 "Ibid., p. 210 (in note) .") President Lyndon B. Summary

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

Created by President Harry S. Truman in 1945 as the Medal of Freedom, the medal was renamed by President John F. Kennedy in 1963 as the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Executive Order 11085 (February 22, 1963) allows the President to recognize "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."

The medal is a white star over a red pentagon, surrounded by five gold eagles. At the star's center is a blue circle with 13 gold stars. The Presidential Medal of Freedom comes in two degrees, with the more prestigious version known as the Presidential Medal of Freedom "with distinction."

There is no formal procedure for nominating and selecting recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The President has wide latitude under Executive Order 11515 (March 13, 1970) to award the medal to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative." Selections often reflect the President's political and personal interests.

Numerous Members of Congress have sent nominations to the President. Some Members have made floor remarks about potential or past recipients and introduced resolutions congratulating honorees or urging the President to recognize a specific individual.

Between 1963 and 2025, the Presidential Medal of Freedom was awarded 674 times to 671 individuals and one group (the Apollo 13 Mission Operations Team); two people (Ellsworth Bunker and Colin Powell) received the medal twice. This report contains a comprehensive list of honorees and indicates the 56 medals known to have been awarded "with distinction."

In establishing the award, he sought to honor civilians who "performed a meritorious act or service which has aided the United States" or one of its allies overseas during wartime, "and for which an award of another United States medal or decoration is considered inappropriate."[1](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn1 "Executive Order 9586, \"The Medal of Freedom,\" 10 Federal Register 8523, July 6, 1945.") During the Korean War, President Truman expanded the medal's eligibility to include actions during "any period of national emergency."[2](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn2 "Executive Order 10336, \"Amendment of Executive Order No. 9586 of July 6, 1945, Establishing the Medal of Freedom,\" 17 Federal Register 2957, April 3, 1952.") It was awarded thousands of times, mostly by federal officials other than the President.[3](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn3 "Bruce Wetterau, The Presidential Medal of Freedom: Winners and Their Achievements (Washington: Congressional Quarterly Inc., 1996), p. 9.")

In his 1955 State of the Union address, President Dwight D. Eisenhower called for "awards of merit … whereby we can honor our fellow citizens who make great contribution to the advancement of our civilization."[4](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn4 "\" Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union \" (January 6, 1955) in U.S. National Archives and Records Service, Office of the Federal Register, Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Dwight D. Eisenhower , 1955, pp. 7-30.") The House twice passed bills to create a Medal for Distinguished Civilian Achievement: H.R. 11923 in the 84 th Congress[5](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn5 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 2, 1956), p. 11609.") and H.R. 488 in the 85 th Congress.[6](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn6 "Congressional Record , vol. 104, part 11 (July 23, 1958), p. 14794.") In each case, the Senate referred the bill to committee and took no further action.[7](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn7 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 3, 1956), p. 11678 and vol. 104, part 11 (July 24, 1958), p. 14895.")

In 1963, President John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 11085 to modify the Medal of Freedom, including by giving it a new name: the Presidential Medal of Freedom. It would now be awarded solely by the President to "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."[8](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn8 "Executive Order 11085, \"The Presidential Medal of Freedom,\" 28 Federal Register 1759, February 22, 1963. Also, in the United States Code at 5 U.S.C. §4504 note.")

President Kennedy said at the time that

in a period when the national government must call upon an increasing portion of the talents and energies of its citizens, it is clearly appropriate to provide ways to recognize and reward the work of persons, within and without the government, who contribute significantly to the quality of American life.[9](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn9 "\" Statement by the President Upon Issuing Order Relating to the Medal of Freedom \" (February 22, 1963) in Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: John F. Kennedy , 1963, pp. 209-210.")

On July 4, 1963, President Kennedy announced the first slate of 31 honorees.[10](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn10 "Ibid., p. 210 (in note) .") President Lyndon B. Johnson presented the initial Presidential Medals of Freedom two weeks after President Kennedy's assassination, with two posthumous additions to the list: Pope John XXIII and President Kennedy.[11](https://www.co

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# President Kennedy's Executive Order 11085: Presidential Medal of Freedom

President Kennedy's Executive Order 11085 (February 22, 1963) re-established the Medal of Freedom as the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

For more information please contact [**Kennedy.Library@nara.gov**](mailto:Kennedy.Library@nara.gov).

## Symbolism of the Design

For years the white star has been displayed throughout the world as the identifying emblem of United States elements in the defense of freedom. It is recognized universally as a symbol of our selfless determination to maintain the freedom and democracy of mankind.

The eagles among the points of the star are of a design of the early Federal period of the United States, and symbolize the supporting strengths and convictions of our own early struggle for freedom.

The constellation of thirteen stars in a field of blue is from the Glory crest of the Coat of Arms of the United States, representing high idealism.

The oak wreath depicts the accolade aspect of the decoration and also emphasizes the quality of strength.

The white stars on the blue background of the ribbon allude to the united states themselves. The multiple, white, five-pointed stars in the blue field of the canton of our flag long have held a conspicuous place as symbols of the states of our Union.

The colors of blue, white, gold and silver are associated with the President's seal and flag.

## Symbolism of the Design

For years the white star has been displayed throughout the world as the identifying emblem of United States elements in the defense of freedom. It is recognized universally as a symbol of our selfless determination to maintain the freedom and democracy of mankind.

The eagles among the points of the star are of a design of the early Federal period of the United States, and symbolize the supporting strengths and convictions of our own early struggle for freedom.

The constellation of thirteen stars in a field of blue is from the Glory crest of the Coat of Arms of the United States, representing high idealism.

The oak wreath depicts the accolade aspect of the decoration and also emphasizes the quality of strength.

The white stars on the blue background of the ribbon allude to the united states themselves. The multiple, white, five-pointed stars in the blue field of the canton of our flag long have held a conspicuous place as symbols of the states of our Union.

The colors of blue, white, gold and silver are associated with the President's seal and flag.

## Symbolism of the Design

For years the white star has been displayed throughout the world as the identifying emblem of United States elements in the defense of freedom. It is recognized universally as a symbol of our selfless determination to maintain the freedom and democracy of mankind.

The eagles among the points of the star are of a design of the early Federal period of the United States, and symbolize the supporting strengths and convictions of our own early struggle for freedom.

The constellation of thirteen stars in a field of blue is from the Glory crest of the Coat of Arms of the United States, representing high idealism.

The oak wreath depicts the accolade aspect of the decoration and also emphasizes the quality of strength.

The white stars on the blue background of the ribbon allude to the united states themselves. The multiple, white, five-pointed stars in the blue field of the canton of our flag long have held a conspicuous place as symbols of the states of our Union.

The colors of blue, white, gold and silver are associated with the President's seal and flag.

## Symbolism of the Design

For years the white star has been displayed throughout the world as the identifying emblem of United States elements in the defense of freedom. It is recognized universally as a symbol of our selfless determination to maintain the freedom and democracy of mankind.

The eagles among the points of the star are of a design of the early Federal period of the United States, and symbolize the supporting strengths and convictions of our own early struggle for freedom.

The constellation of thirteen stars in a field of blue is from the Glory crest of the Coat of Arms of the United States, representing high idealism.

The oak wreath depicts the accolade aspect of the decoration and also emphasizes the quality of strength.

The white stars on the blue background of the ribbon allude to the united states themselves. The multiple, white, five-pointed stars in the blue field of the canton of our flag long have held a conspicuous place as symbols of the states of our Union.

The colors of blue, white, gold and silver are associated with the President's seal and flag.

Most Mercurian craters [[Planetary nomenclature|are named after]] famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [[Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature]], all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named. Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as \"basins\" ''(also see {{Section link||Terminology}})''.[https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/Projects/PlanetaryMapping/DIGGEOL/mercury/h7/h7.pdf H-7 text\\_all.word] {{As of|2025}}, there are 444 named Mercurian craters, a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [[List of craters on the Moon|lunar]], [[List of craters on Mars|Martian]] and [[List of craters on Venus|Venerian]] craters.{{efn|name=WGPSN-Dropped}} Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [[Callisto (moon)|Callisto]] ([[List of craters on Callisto|141]]), [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]] ([[List of craters on Ganymede|131]]), [[Rhea (moon)|Rhea]] (128), [[4 Vesta|Vesta]] (90), [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] (90), [[Dione (moon)|Dione]] (73), [[Iapetus (moon)|Iapetus]] (58), [[Enceladus (moon)|Enceladus]] (53), [[Tethys (moon)|Tethys]] (50) and [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] ([[List of craters on Europa|41]]). According to the rules by IAU's [[Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature]], all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named. Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as \"basins\" ''(also see {{Section link||Terminology}})''.[https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/Projects/PlanetaryMapping/DIGGEOL/mercury/h7/h7.pdf H-7 text\\_all.word] {{As of|2025}}, there are 444 named Mercurian craters, a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [[List of craters on the Moon|lunar]], [[List of craters on Mars|Martian]] and [[List of craters on Venus|Venerian]] craters.{{efn|name=WGPSN-Dropped}} Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [[Callisto (moon)|Callisto]] ([[List of craters on Callisto|141]]), [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]] ([[List of craters on Ganymede|131]]), [[Rhea (moon)|Rhea]] (128), [[4 Vesta|Vesta]] (90), [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] (90), [[Dione (moon)|Dione]] (73), [[Iapetus (moon)|Iapetus]] (58), [[Enceladus (moon)|Enceladus]] (53), [[Tethys (moon)|Tethys]] (50) and [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] ([[List of craters on Europa|41]]). Most Mercurian craters [[Planetary nomenclature|are named after]] famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [[Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature]], all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named. Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as \"basins\" ''(also see {{Section link||Terminology}})''.[https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/Projects/PlanetaryMapping/DIGGEOL/mercury/h7/h7.pdf H-7 text\\_all.word] {{As of|2025}}, there are 444 named Mercurian craters, a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [[List of craters on the Moon|lunar]], [[List of craters on Mars|Martian]] and [[List of craters on Venus|Venerian]] craters.{{efn|name=WGPSN-Dropped}} Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [[Callisto (moon)|Callisto]] ([[List of craters on Callisto|141]]), [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]] ([[List of craters on Ganymede|131]]), [[Rhea (moon)|Rhea]] (128), [[4 Vesta|Vesta]] (90), [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] (90), [[Dione (moon)|Dione]] (73), [[Iapetus (moon)|Iapetus]] (58), [[Enceladus (moon)|Enceladus]] (53), [[Tethys (moon)|Tethys]] (50) and [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] ([[List of craters on Europa|41]]). Most Mercurian craters [[Planetary nomenclature|are named after]] famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [[Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature]], all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named. Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as \"basins\" ''(also see {{Section link||Terminology}})''.[https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/Projects/PlanetaryMapping/DIGGEOL/mercury/h7/h7.pdf H-7 text\\_all.word] {{As of|2025}}, there are 444 named Mercurian craters, a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [[List of craters on the Moon|lunar]], [[List of craters on Mars|Martian]] and [[List of craters on Venus|Venerian]] craters.{{efn|name=WGPSN-Dropped}} Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [[Callisto (moon)|Callisto]] ([[List of craters on Callisto|141]]), [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]] ([[List of craters on Ganymede|131]]), [[Rhea (moon)|Rhea]] (128), [[4 Vesta|Vesta]] (90), [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] (90), [[Dione (moon)|Dione]] (73), [[Iapetus (moon)|Iapetus]] (58), [[Enceladus (moon)|Enceladus]] (53), [[Tethys (moon)|Tethys]] (50) and [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] ([[List of craters on Europa|41]]). ## Search method v007

Define X and Y exactly, including entity unit, exclusions, effective dates, eligible subtypes and group-membership rules. Start sequentially with one X-only search, one Y-only search and one conjunction search, using the user's broad predicate wording rather than a familiar subtype. Maintain deduplicated X/Y frontiers and an identity/evidence ledger. Also maintain a compact scope ledger: for each discovery query record added restrictions not required by the hunt (subtype, occupation, geography, era, source or familiar-name terms). A successful restricted query does not establish coverage of its parent category. Derive a few meaningful sibling partitions from source taxonomies or the eligibility definition; do not invent an exhaustive cross-product or enumerate a whole census by default. Run short discovery/check rounds, prioritizing expected verified additions per total resolution cost. Each round's neglected-subtype or reverse-frontier probe must address a specific untested scope-ledger cell or remove a recorded accidental restriction; merely paraphrasing a prior conjunction does not qualify. Check source-backed candidates on Parallel for only unresolved predicates, supplying identity and existing evidence. Use small affordable batches, price every candidate, and do not recheck established facts. No result means unresolved, not false; reject only on contradiction or an exhaustive applicable source. Escalate promising ambiguous or conflicting cases individually to Exa. After two discovery searches add no plausible identities, prohibit synonymous conjunction searches and perform a residual-scope pass: identify the most consequential restriction accumulated so far, try a sibling subtype or unrestricted parent on the opposite frontier, then resolve resulting candidates before further discovery. Reserve at least 35% of initial funds for evidence and stop discovery whenever pending checks require the remaining funds. Before submitting with spare funds, perform up to three affordable residual probes covering distinct untested restrictions or source partitions, retaining enough funds to verify their likely candidates. Stop this pass after two probes add neither candidates nor useful evidence; do not spend merely to exhaust the budget. Finish with identity, predicate, subtype and effective-date audits; submit supported intersections only and never infer completeness from saturation.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.

Price candidate batches as the sum of queries and provider charges; fewer results are not presumed cheaper. Exa alone with 4 results for selected unresolved identities where ambiguity, conflicting evidence or inaccessibility warrants the higher cost. At most one initial Exa discovery probe after Parallel stagnation, continued only if it contributes useful new identities or evidence. Try a genuinely different scope partition on Parallel before buying provider diversity for a repetitive query. Authoritative-domain filters are for targeted evidence, not general frontier coverage; relax failed filters. Use publication-date filters only when publication date itself determines eligibility, and verify effective dates in content.

Reuse cached source facts. Fetch authoritative pages that can settle missing identity or predicates, and useful multi-candidate lists, rather than every result. When a list is used for scope coverage, inspect its stated subtype, date range and pagination/section links; an excerpt or one section is not an exhausted category. Summary

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

Created by President Harry S. Truman in 1945 as the Medal of Freedom, the medal was renamed by President John F. Kennedy in 1963 as the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Executive Order 11085 (February 22, 1963) allows the President to recognize "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."

The medal is a white star over a red pentagon, surrounded by five gold eagles. At the star's center is a blue circle with 13 gold stars. The Presidential Medal of Freedom comes in two degrees, with the more prestigious version known as the Presidential Medal of Freedom "with distinction."

There is no formal procedure for nominating and selecting recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The President has wide latitude under Executive Order 11515 (March 13, 1970) to award the medal to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative." Selections often reflect the President's political and personal interests.

Numerous Members of Congress have sent nominations to the President. Some Members have made floor remarks about potential or past recipients and introduced resolutions congratulating honorees or urging the President to recognize a specific individual.

Between 1963 and 2025, the Presidential Medal of Freedom was awarded 674 times to 671 individuals and one group (the Apollo 13 Mission Operations Team); two people (Ellsworth Bunker and Colin Powell) received the medal twice. This report contains a comprehensive list of honorees and indicates the 56 medals known to have been awarded "with distinction."

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html)In July 1945, President Harry S. Truman issued an executive order, near the end of World War II, to create the Medal of Freedom. In establishing the award, he sought to honor civilians who "performed a meritorious act or service which has aided the United States" or one of its allies overseas during wartime, "and for which an award of another United States medal or decoration is considered inappropriate."[1](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn1 "Executive Order 9586, \"The Medal of Freedom,\" 10 Federal Register 8523, July 6, 1945.") During the Korean War, President Truman expanded the medal's eligibility to include actions during "any period of national emergency."[2](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn2 "Executive Order 10336, \"Amendment of Executive Order No. 9586 of July 6, 1945, Establishing the Medal of Freedom,\" 17 Federal Register 2957, April 3, 1952.") It was awarded thousands of times, mostly by federal officials other than the President.[3](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn3 "Bruce Wetterau, The Presidential Medal of Freedom: Winners and Their Achievements (Washington: Congressional Quarterly Inc., 1996), p. 9.")

In his 1955 State of the Union address, President Dwight D. Eisenhower called for "awards of merit … whereby we can honor our fellow citizens who make great contribution to the advancement of our civilization."[4](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn4 "\" Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union \" (January 6, 1955) in U.S. National Archives and Records Service, Office of the Federal Register, Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Dwight D. Eisenhower , 1955, pp. 7-30.") The House twice passed bills to create a Medal for Distinguished Civilian Achievement: H.R. 11923 in the 84 th Congress[5](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn5 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 2, 1956), p. 11609.") and H.R. 488 in the 85 th Congress.[6](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn6 "Congressional Record , vol. 104, part 11 (July 23, 1958), p. 14794.") In each case, the Senate referred the bill to committee and took no further action.[7](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn7 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 3, 1956), p. 11678 and vol. 104, part 11 (July 24, 1958), p. 14895.")

In 1963, President John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 11085 to modify the Medal of Freedom, including by giving it a new name: the Presidential Medal of Freedom. It would now be awarded solely by the President to "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."[8](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn8 "Executive Order 11085, \"The Presidential Medal of Freedom,\" 28 Federal Register 1759, February 22, 1963. Also, in the United States Code at 5 U.S.C. §4504 note.")

President Kennedy said at the time that

in a period when the national government must call upon an increasing portion of the talents and energies of its citizens, it is clearly appropriate to provide ways to recognize and reward the work of persons, within and without the government, who contribute significantly to the quality of American life.[9](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn9 "\" Statement by the President Upon Issuing Order Relating to the Medal of Freedom \" (February 22, 1963) in Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: John F. Kennedy , 1963, pp. 209-210.")

On July 4, 1963, President Kennedy announced the first slate of 31 honorees.[10](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/HTML/R47639.web.html#fn10 "Ibid., p. 210 (in note) .") From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# President Kennedy's Executive Order 11085: Presidential Medal of Freedom

President Kennedy's Executive Order 11085 (February 22, 1963) re-established the Medal of Freedom as the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

For more information please contact [**Kennedy.Library@nara.gov**](mailto:Kennedy.Library@nara.gov).

## Recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom, 6 December 1963

Thirty one individuals were awarded the medal on December 6, 1963 by President Lyndon Baines Johnson:

Miss Marian Anderson   
Mr. Pablo Casals   
Miss Genevieve Caulfield   
Dr. John F. Enders   
Mr. Karl Holton   
Mr. Robert J. Kiphuth   
Mr. Edwin H. Land   
Governor Herbert H. Lehman (in absentia)   
Mr. J. Clifford MacDonald (Mrs. MacDonald received the award on behalf of her deceased husband)   
Mr. George Meany   
Professor Alexander Meiklejohn   
Mr. Ludwig Mies van der Rohe   
Mr. Clarence B. Randall   
Mr. Rudolf Serkin   
Mr. Edward Steichen   
Professor George W. Taylor   
Dr. Alan T. Waterman   
Mr. Mark S. Watson   
Mrs. Annie D. Wauneka   
Mr. E.B. White   
Mr. Edmund Wilson   
Mr. Thornton Wilder   
Mr. Andrew Wyeth

Those who received the award with Special Distinction:

Mr. Ellsworth Bunker   
Dr. Ralph J. Bunche   
Dr. James B. Conant   
Governor Luis Muñoz Marín   
Mr. Robert A. Lovett   
Mr. Jean Monnet   
Mr. Justice Felix Frankfurter   
Mr. John J. McCloy

President Johnson conferred the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously on His Holiness, Pope John XXIII. He also awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously to President John Fitzgerald Kennedy.

## Symbolism of the Design

For years the white star has been displayed throughout the world as the identifying emblem of United States elements in the defense of freedom. It is recognized universally as a symbol of our selfless determination to maintain the freedom and democracy of mankind.

The eagles among the points of the star are of a design of the early Federal period of the United States, and symbolize the supporting strengths and convictions of our own early struggle for freedom.

The constellation of thirteen stars in a field of blue is from the Glory crest of the Coat of Arms of the United States, representing high idealism.

The oak wreath depicts the accolade aspect of the decoration and also emphasizes the quality of strength.

The white stars on the blue background of the ribbon allude to the united states themselves. The multiple, white, five-pointed stars in the blue field of the canton of our flag long have held a conspicuous place as symbols of the states of our Union.

The colors of blue, white, gold and silver are associated with the President's seal and flag.

*Source: Papers of John F. Kennedy. Presidential Papers. President's Office Files. Subjects. Most Mercurian craters [[Planetary nomenclature|are named after]] famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [[Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature]], all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named. Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as \"basins\" ''(also see {{Section link||Terminology}})''.[https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/Projects/PlanetaryMapping/DIGGEOL/mercury/h7/h7.pdf H-7 text\\_all.word] {{As of|2025}}, there are 444 named Mercurian craters, a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [[List of craters on the Moon|lunar]], [[List of craters on Mars|Martian]] and [[List of craters on Venus|Venerian]] craters.{{efn|name=WGPSN-Dropped}} Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [[Callisto (moon)|Callisto]] ([[List of craters on Callisto|141]]), [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]] ([[List of craters on Ganymede|131]]), [[Rhea (moon)|Rhea]] (128), [[4 Vesta|Vesta]] (90), [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] (90), [[Dione (moon)|Dione]] (73), [[Iapetus (moon)|Iapetus]] (58), [[Enceladus (moon)|Enceladus]] (53), [[Tethys (moon)|Tethys]] (50) and [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] ([[List of craters on Europa|41]]).
